content: Souroti (Greek: Σουρωτή) is a rural village situated 25 kilometers (16 miles) outside the city of Thessaloniki in Greece. It is particularly renowned in Greece for its bottled mineral water. Administratively, the village is part of the municipality of Vasilika. History Souroti is an immigrant village, one of many established in Greek Macedonia following the Balkan Wars and the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. Before 1912, the area was known as Surukli, a name derived from the Turkish word suru, meaning herd. At that time, the land was owned by five Turkish landlords (referred to as Τσιφλικάδες), who later sold it to Jewish buyers from Thessaloniki. The first Greek settlers in the area were the Christos Lolas family, originally shepherds from Vlasti in the Kozani prefecture. They sold their sheep to purchase the land from the Jewish owners. In 1914, forty families of Arvanites arrived from Mandritsa in North Thrace, fleeing a Bulgarian invasion of their home village. These settlers were bilingual, speaking both Greek and Arvanitika, and primarily engaged in silk production, utilizing the local mulberry trees. In 1922, following the population exchange between Greece and Turkey, approximately 48 families from Asia Minor arrived in Souroti. These families originated from places such as Izmir (Σμύρνη), Aydin (Αηδίνι), Bursa (Προύσσα), Kyos (Κύος), Mudanya (Μουδανιά), and Eastern Thrace. They were educated individuals who brought their own traditions and worked in Souroti as silk producers, olive oil producers, and vine dressers. Between 1928 and 1930, additional Vlach shepherds from Vlasti, along with 4-5 families of Sarakatsanoi (Σαρακατσάνοι), settled in the area. The Greek state distributed land to the immigrants in 1914 and again in 1932. Modern Establishment The community of Souroti was officially established and recognized by the Greek state on September 20, 1947. Since then, the village has experienced steady development, with agriculture and the bottling of mineral water as its main productive activities. In 1997, during a major reorganization of local self-government under the Kapodistrias Plan initiated by the Greek government, Souroti merged with the municipality of Vasilika, along with Agia Paraskevi, Agios Antonios, Libadi, Monopigado, and Peristera. In recent years, people from nearby Thessaloniki have been moving to the area, which is expected to transform into a suburb of Thessaloniki. Discovery of the Mineral Water Spring During the Ottoman Empire, the area around the current bottling factory was a swamp, and the mineral water spring was unknown. During the 1915 military campaigns of World War I, French troops camping in the then-called Surukli mapped the spring and constructed a rudimentary bottling facility. In 1917, Serbian troops also camped in the area and built a new bottling facility, naming the water Sour Water (Serbian: Kisela Voda). In 1918, the Lolas family appropriated and refurbished the facility. By 1925, George Chonaios took over the Lolas enterprise, operating the facility as a private business while allocating 5% of the profits to the local community. In 1998, the company went public, experiencing rapid development and becoming one of the most popular mineral water brands in Greece. Quality of the Mineral Water Souroti water is recognized as a sub-acidic sparkling mineral water rich in calcium and magnesium, in accordance with Greek legislation (Government Gazette 600/1-8-1991, Decision No. 4). It is also included in the European Union's list of Natural Mineral Waters. Initially, in the early 20th century, the water was naturally sparkling. While it retains its original mineral composition, carbon dioxide is now added during bottling. The water is sourced from a container approximately 150 meters underground. Its excellent quality is attributed to the rock formations of Mount Anthemounta, which consist of semi-metamorphic, metamorphic, and igneous rocks. As the water flows slowly through these rocks, it is filtered and enriched with beneficial elements, giving it a unique mineral composition and distinctive taste. The spring water is cold, maintaining a steady temperature of around 16°C. Souroti water is characterized by its high magnesium content, an ideal calcium-to-magnesium ratio, and low sodium and nitrate levels. It also contains potassium, fluoride, and valuable trace elements such as iron, copper, manganese, lithium, selenium, chromium, and zinc. The water has an exceptional taste, is pleasant to drink, and supports the functioning of the digestive and urinary systems, offering several health benefits. One liter of Souroti water meets one-fourth of the body's daily calcium and magnesium requirements. These qualities distinguish it from soda water, which is ordinary potable water with added sodium bicarbonate to mimic the properties of natural mineral water.
